title: 1-01 Tidecrown
body:
### Background and Hook(s)

- 

### Characters and Locations

- **Primarch Tethys Aquarius** (LN female merfolk, Tidecrown’s Leader). Tall and regal, with a flowing silver-and-black cape that sways in the water like ink in a current. Her eyes are a striking pale gold, and she never blinks while speaking. Keeps Tidecrown stable at any cost, even through suppression of truth.
- **Magister Ilren Vos** (TN female human, PACT Operations Coordinator). Ilren Vos delivers the standing morning briefing at the start of each session. Her briefings are factual, neutral, and non-prescriptive. She presents developments as status updates rather than calls to action, outlining constraints, uncertainties, and observed changes without assigning priority or judgment. Vos is reliable, informed, and deliberately noncommittal. She answers questions precisely but never speculates unless pressed. If her tone shifts from procedural calm to concern, it signals a genuine escalation in the world state.
- **Dr. Lilly Fellwater** (CN female merfolk scholar, Head Scientist and Animal Behaviorist). Slender, with skin the pale blue of deep glacial ice and hair braided into long cords tipped with tiny glass beads that chime softly when she moves. Always smells faintly of kelp and saltwater tinctures. Obsessive about her kuo-toa research, fiercely protective of her “subjects”.
- **Dr. Karrun Deepwake** (LN male merfolk healer, Head of Tidecrown Infirmary). Broad chest and muscular arms, scales a deep cobalt blue; wears a necklace of driftwood charms. Left fin is scarred and partially torn, making his swim slightly lopsided. Treats everyone equally.
- **Sergeant Caelis Dorn** (NE male merfolk, Head of Tidecrown Security). Weathered face with one cloudy, milky-white eye; armor inlaid with tarnished silver wave motifs. Speaks in a gravelly monotone, as if every word costs effort. Oversees city guard rotations, known for “getting results” by any means necessary.
- **Chief Gregaarious Lonadar** (male Gnome Magewright, Chief Engineer). The primary engineer who keeps the base afloat, and who Mith works with routinely. Has a haughty voice, and is as pedantic as possible. All of the kuo-toa workers pronounce his wrong (as "gregarious"), and he's constantly correcting them.
- **Commander Vorthak ir’Ssar** (LE male sahuagin war captain, summit delegate). Broad-shouldered with jagged fin crests dyed crimson, and a deep scar running across his snout. Wears shark-tooth necklaces that clack ominously when he moves. Proud, quick to take offense, respects strength above diplomacy.
- **Mithral (Mith)** (LN male warforged quartermaster). With his exquisite attention to detail, Mith keeps PACT's storeroom humming. He meticulously catalogues every item, and knows exactly where everything belongs and what's checked out to whom at all times. His stone and metallic construction causes him to almost blend into the background, which he often prefers, as it means he can focus on his work. His name comes from his heart literally made of mithral (the most interesting part about him).
- **Tessira Vane** (CG female half-elf shopkeeper, Pearl Market merchant). Freckled from sun exposure, with a shock of white hair dyed with streaks of sea-green. Always wears a heavy leather apron with pockets full of coins, shells, and curious trinkets. Gossip hub, knows the rhythms of Tidecrown commerce.
- **Skarek** (CN male sahuagin tailor). A sahuagin exile and the proprietor of Skarek's Sartorial on the Tidecrown Concourse. He was formerly an intelligence operative embedded in Tidecrown under the Ra'har of Hal'syra, gathering information on neutral-port politics and removing problems quietly when the Sha'rei required it. He was administratively unmade — not formally exiled, simply erased from standing — after he failed to complete an assassination in Tidecrown under circumstances he describes differently every time he's asked. He stayed because Tidecrown's neutrality meant no one could legally remove him, and because his operational knowledge of the city made it the only place he could survive; the tailoring, forced on him as cover during his embedded years, is now the one thing that is entirely his own. He is not a pacifist — he is a predator who has chosen, for now, not to hunt, and the distinction is legible to anyone paying attention.
- **Orvel Dast** (LN male human, chef). Compact and pale, with close-cropped gray hair and hands that show no scars despite decades of knife work. He speaks rarely, precisely, and never defends his food; if you don't understand it, that's your problem. He sources exclusively from live capture — nothing frozen, nothing farmed — and has cultivated relationships with both locathah trappers and, quietly, sahuagin suppliers, which raises questions he declines to answer.
- **Vella Pisces** (N female merfolk receptionist. A middle-aged triton woman who has staffed the Tidecrown reception desks longer than anyone can remember, rotating between all three with a coffee-shop efficiency that makes it look easy. She calls everyone "sweetie" regardless of rank — admirals and kuo-toa laborers get the same treatment — and delivers information with the cheerful finality of someone sliding a plate across a counter and moving on. Her uniform is always immaculate, her smile never wavers, and she will tell you exactly what you need and nothing else, hon. The neurosis surfaces only in the details: she straightens things that aren't crooked, has a desk rotation she'd never admit exists, and finishes people's sentences a half-beat early under her breath.

#### ★1: Tidecrown General
 - [x]  ✅ 2026-02-02
- Sits low on the ocean, heavy and deliberate, like it expects to submerge at any moment.
- Built wide, not tall — a platform, not a tower or city (although underwater levels do exist).
- All lighting is embedded into structure seams, never freestanding or ornamental.
- No visible engines or propulsion—only contained systems doing quiet work.
- Magic is audible and tactile: hums, vibrations, pressure changes.
- Every major space feels over-reinforced, as if diplomacy routinely goes wrong here.
- Windows are thick, diagnostic, and slightly distorting—the ocean is always “measured,” never scenic.
- Power sources are centralized and dangerous, but deliberately hidden behind layers of safety and labor.
- Residential spaces feel borrowed from the machine, not separate from it.
- Nothing flashes, arcs, or crackles unless it’s a controlled failure state.
- The base feels expensive to operate and clearly requires constant staffing.
- Designed to lock down, seal, and survive rather than inspire or intimidate.
- No overt religious or symbolic iconography—authority comes from engineering competence.
- The sea is omnipresent but never romanticized—a pressure, not a vista.
- The entire structure reads as infrastructure elevated to political significance, not a monument.

##### Exterior
>The structure sits heavy on the water, broad and segmented, its dark stone and metal hull rising only a few stories above the waves. Soft lines of contained light trace seams and pylons, steady and deliberate, with no flicker or flourish. The sea laps against reinforced edges as if testing them, and the base does not respond—anchored, balanced, and clearly built to endure more than calm weather.

##### The Concourse Spine
- This is the main circulation artery, running laterally through the core of the base. The space is wide, reinforced, and subtly curved, with ribbed bulkheads and inlaid sigil-lines embedded in the floor like transit markings.
- A number of market shop shells are available here, with only a few currently occupied:
	- **Temple of Adeus**.
	- **We Three Kings**. Lotor's restaurant.
	- **Pearl Market**. A gift-shop like general market run by Tessira Vane.
	- **Skarek's Sartorial**. A seemingly simple clothing shop run by a charismatic but secretive sahuagin. Obviously inspired by Garek from Star Trek: DS9.
	- **Fathom**. A sleek, expensive restaurant on the Concourse built around floor-to-ceiling pressurized glass tanks running the full length of the dining room — eels, crustaceans, cephalopods, reef fish, and more exotic specimens, all alive and on display. The aesthetic is clinical and beautiful: low blue-white light, bare stone surfaces, no ornamentation except the tanks themselves. The menu doesn't exist. You walk the tanks with a host, point, and the kitchen decides how it dies and how it's prepared. Fathom opened without announcement and was full within the week.
		- **Senri** (N female triton, host). Tall, unhurried, and dressed in matte charcoal with no jewelry. She guides guests along the tanks with quiet authority. `encounter: 1: Abjurer`
		- **Orvel Dast** (LN male human, chef). Compact and pale, with close-cropped gray hair and hands that show no scars despite decades of knife work. He speaks rarely, precisely, and never defends his food; if you don't understand it, that's your problem. He sources exclusively from live capture — nothing frozen, nothing farmed — and has cultivated relationships with both locathah trappers and, quietly, sahuagin suppliers, which raises questions he declines to answer. `encounter: 1: Veteran`
		- **Tanks**: Boiling Eels (Ghomuth), Shining Seahorses (Maris), Bioluminescent Octopus (Cordelia)
		- Security staff added after the night attack on their tanks. `encounter: 3: Veteran`

##### The Civic Vault
- Set deep within the structure (directly beneath the Concourse Spine), this chamber feels insulated and deliberately isolated. The walls are thick with layered materials and overlapping wards that dampen sound, magic, and divination without fully negating them. Translation and recording magic is built into the architecture itself, invisible but ever-present.
- The offices of the Primarch, PACT, and any other civic bodies are located here. The infirmary and security office are here as well.

##### The Habitation Level
- Living quarters are compact, modular, and clearly designed for long-term occupation. Corridors feature pressure seals, reinforced doors, and emergency glyphs that suggest rapid lockdown or submersion protocols. Rooms rely on quiet, domestic magic: temperature-regulating stone, filtered elemental water, and adaptive lighting.
- There are levels of residences further under the water too, primarily for the working class.

##### The Observation Galleries
- These chambers are lined with thick, faceted crystal windows framed by etched metal. The view outward is intentionally mediated—slightly distorted by arcane refraction and overlaid with faint diagnostic readouts showing pressure, structural integrity, and environmental conditions. The world outside is visible, but always framed as something hostile, distant, and measured rather than conquered.
- The Galleries are divided into public and private research areas. The public areas are closest to the Concourse Spine, and are a common draw for visitors who seek to see what's under the sea. The private research areas are available to a variety of scientists, including the kuo-toa research of Dr. Lilly Fellwater.

##### The Elemental Core
- This is the loudest, most volatile space in the base. Bound water and air elementals churn within containment rings, their motion translated into stabilization, power, and environmental control. Arcane conduits spark and pulse in response, and warning glyphs flare periodically as part of normal operation.

##### The Maintenance Decks
- Often overlooked, these decks define the base’s true character. Narrow corridors packed with conduits, valves, and access panels are staffed by technicians and magewrights performing continuous upkeep.
- The docks for Tidecrown staff and residents (as opposed to the diplomat docks, which is off the Concourse Spine) is here as well, with three different types of sea vessels available to rent.

#### ★1: Couaxolotl Shrine
 - [ ]  
- Based on The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan (from Tales from the Yawning Portal). Changed tomb imagery and poison traps to celestial imagery and radiant energy. Then structured the best area content into three tiers of essentially five-room dungeons.
- The first (top) tier is fully flooded (and ruined in appearance), and mostly open to the surrounding sea - the players are able to swim right up and into the shrine. This tier ends at a pressure lock that transitions down into the second tier - which is entirely dry (but still a little run down in appearance). The third tier is deepest and most pristine - the proper Temple of the Couaxolotl.
- The Shrine is protected by an **Arcane Leviathan** (CR 16) - a ship of the Aventi who are protecting the Shrine from anyone they deem as unworthy (anyone who can't manage to either defeat them in honorable combat or learn about their true nature/history).

`encounter: 1: Arcane Leviathan`

##### TIER I — THE DROWNED OUTER SHRINE
_Fully flooded. Open to the surrounding sea. Structurally compromised._

###### C1. The Sunken Vestibule
>Stone pillars rise from the seafloor into the vaulted ceiling of a drowned temple hall, their surfaces softened by age and drifting silt. Pale green light filters faintly from above, illuminating six recessed alcoves along the walls, each holding a miniature carved scene. At the center of the chamber, a circular well drops several feet deeper, its rim etched with spiraling constellations and tidal motifs. The water here is strangely still, undisturbed by the currents of the surrounding sea. The eastern wall is smooth and undecorated, as though intentionally sealed.

**Based on:** TFtYP Areas 54, 1
- The chamber is approximately 60 feet long and 20 feet wide, sloping gently downward from west to east. A 10-foot-wide circular well sits at the center, 5 feet deeper than the surrounding floor. Visibility is limited to 20 feet due to suspended silt, and there is no current inside the hall.
- Six alcoves (three per wall) contain carved dioramas with removable figures. Removing any figure and placing it on the floor causes it to enlarge into a Medium Radiant Memory Construct (use Animated Armor with a swim speed). Constructs defend the room only. A Religion or History check of an individual alcove may reveal any or all of the information below each bullet (at DM discretion).
	- **Alcove I — The Thunder Sea (Ancient Age)**. A vast, calm ocean stretches in smooth carved planes. At its center coils a large celestial axolotl beneath clear skies, its presence visibly shaping currents in gentle arcs. Marine life flourishes around it in ordered harmony.
		- The Couaxolotl ruled the Thunder Sea in an age when it was calm and stable. The sea only became violent and storm-wracked after the Couaxolotl’s decline.
	- **Alcove II — The Dark Sea (Ancient Age)**. Towering giant citadels rise from deep ocean trenches. Massive stone forges and structured cities are carved into abyssal cliffs. Sea life thrives around carefully constructed settlements, showing the Giants as organized rulers of a powerful, industrious sea.
		- The Giants controlled the Dark Sea at the height of their civilization. Their mastery extended into planar engineering and large-scale magical works.
	- **Alcove III — The Barren Sea (Ancient Age)**. A vibrant ocean filled with strange life forms, including dreamlike creatures with elongated shapes and flowing forms. Kuo-Toa gather in structured ritual circles along coral cities, with spiraling motifs carved into the sea’s surface representing open dream-paths to Dal Quor.
		- The Barren Sea was once fertile and connected to Dal Quor. The Quor-Toa actively maintained these dream conduits, until they were inadvertently wiped out by the Giants.
	- **Alcove IV — The Severing of the Dream**. Giant figures raise crystalline monoliths along a shoreline while spiral dream-rifts fracture above the sea. The carved spiral between ocean and sky visibly splits apart.
		- The Giants severed the connection between the material world and Dal Quor. This act destabilized the Barren Sea permanently.
	- **Alcove V — The Collapse of the Quor-Toa Civilization**. Coral structures crumble. Kuo-Toa figures fall or scatter as dream-creatures vanish from the carved sea. The once-vibrant waters are shown empty and smooth.
		- The Quor-Toa (People of Dreams) civilization collapsed after the severing, leading eventually to the modern day Kuo-Toa (Fallen People).
	- **Alcove VI — The Dimming of the Thunder Sea**. The celestial axolotl’s form fades into constellations overhead. The calm sea becomes carved with jagged lines suggesting storms and chaos.
		- The Couaxolotl eventually died out or withdrew from the world. Their absence led directly to the Thunder Sea becoming unstable and violent.
- The central well contains a carved Celestial Pilgrim (Couaxolotl) holding a looped silver crook. Removing the figure animates it as described above; once defeated, the crook remains intact and functions as a key.
- The eastern wall is a seamless stone door. A concealed keyhole beneath the keystone can be detected with DC 20 Perception. Inserting the crook unlocks the door with a quarter turn.
- Forcing the door requires dealing 40 damage (AC 17). On any failed Strength check by 5 or more, falling debris deals 1d6 bludgeoning to creatures within 10 feet.

`encounter: 1: Animated Armor`

###### C2. Hall of Thrashing Reeds
>The corridor narrows and slopes more sharply downward, its walls carved in repeating vertical ridges that resemble bundled reeds or ribbed stone columns. The grooves run floor to ceiling on both sides, evenly spaced and unnervingly uniform. The passage descends toward a set of bronze double doors at the far end, their surfaces dulled but intact beneath the water. No visible mechanisms or handles mark the walls.

**Based on:** TFtYP Area 2
- The corridor is 40 feet long and descends approximately 10 feet toward the eastern bronze doors. The carved vertical ridges along both walls conceal hinged stone rods recessed flush with the surface.
- Careful inspection of the walls reveals faint hinge seams and abrasion marks along the floor. A DC 15 Perception check while moving cautiously detects the danger below before it triggers.
- When a creature passes the midpoint of the corridor, concealed mechanisms release and multiple stone rods swing outward from both walls in the central 15-foot section. Each creature in that zone takes 2d6 bludgeoning damage and must succeed on a DC 13 Strength saving throw or be driven 10 feet downslope toward the doors.
- The rods remain extended for 1 minute before retracting. While extended, the corridor narrows to roughly 2 feet wide, requiring creatures to squeeze to pass through.
- The mechanism can be disabled with a DC 15 Dexterity check using thieves’ tools, requiring 5 minutes of steady work at one wall seam.
- The bronze double doors at the eastern end are heavy but functional and open inward without additional keys or traps, leading to Room 3.

###### C3. Guardian Pool of the Luminous Drifter
>The corridor widens into a circular chamber whose stone walls are streaked white with mineral deposits. The water here is cloudy and faintly milky, clinging in sluggish layers around the floor. A soft phosphorescent glow emanates from the far wall, where something large and pale adheres to the stone like a living mantle. Along the eastern wall, an alcove fountain trickles cloudy fluid into the chamber, its basin crusted with chalky residue. The passage continues beyond the glowing shape.

**Based on:** TFtYP Areas 3, 11
- The water in this chamber is saturated with alkaline lime leached from the stone. A creature that remains in this room for more than 10 minutes begins to feel irritation; after 30 minutes, exposed skin takes 1 acid damage per minute until rinsed with fresh water. Cloth and soft leather begin to degrade after prolonged exposure (use the degradation logic from Area 5).
- The eastern alcove contains a fountain basin filled with highly concentrated lime solution. Contact with the basin’s fluid deals 1 acid damage per round of exposure. At the bottom of the basin rests an amulet worth 65 gp (reskinned as a stylized axolotl medallion), which Tecuziztecatl recognizes and values.
- The phosphorescent figure is Tecuziztecatl, a massive intelligent slug adhered to the wall (use Giant Slug statistics; add 30-foot swim speed). He glows faintly and speaks in a deep, resonant voice, referring to himself as “Lord of the Chamber” and boasting of his dominion.
- Tecuziztecatl is vain, theatrical, and deeply proud. He demands tribute or flattery before allowing passage, but prefers conversation to combat. He enjoys being admired and may exaggerate his importance in the shrine’s hierarchy.
- If attacked, he fights aggressively but will attempt to bargain if reduced below half hit points. If given the amulet from the basin, he becomes temporarily cooperative and allows safe passage.
- The water’s alkalinity makes extended combat dangerous. Each minute spent fighting in the chamber continues to count toward the 30-minute exposure threshold. The exit passage continues downward beyond Tecuziztecatl’s wall, still fully flooded.

`encounter: 1: Giant Slug`

###### C4. The Tidal Threshold
>The passage narrows before ending at a massive circular bronze door set into the stone, its surface etched with spiraling tidal motifs. The metal is intact and tightly sealed into a carved stone ring, with faint mineral streaks radiating outward like frozen currents. Small vents carved into the surrounding stone release thin threads of cloudy water that drift lazily upward. Beyond the door, the corridor continues deeper into shadow.

**Based on:** TFtYP Area 12
- The bronze door is pressure-sealed within a circular stone housing. It is not locked, but it resists opening due to internal water pressure held by a counterbalanced mechanism.
- Opening the door without preparation releases a sudden lateral surge as high-pressure water vents through the side channels. All creatures within 15 feet must succeed on a DC 14 Strength saving throw or be hurled 15 feet backward and take 2d6 bludgeoning damage from being slammed against the stone corridor.
- After the initial surge, a strong localized current persists for 1 minute in a 20-foot radius around the doorway. Movement toward the door during this time requires a DC 12 Athletics check each round.
- Careful inspection (DC 15 Perception) reveals small rotary relief carvings around the circular frame. Turning these carved tidal glyphs in sequence (DC 14 Intelligence-based check to interpret) equalizes the pressure gradually, preventing the surge.
- If the party triggered the surge, the noise echoes heavily through the flooded complex. You may have Tecuziztecatl react vocally or send curious commentary echoing down the corridor.
- Once opened and stabilized, the bronze door remains ajar. The passage beyond slopes downward into a vertical shaft leading to Room 5.

###### C5. The Celestial Pressure Lock
>The shaft widens into a circular chamber carved with spiraling constellations and tidal bands that wrap around the walls. The water is still here, thicker and more opaque, and the stone bears heavy white mineral crust along every seam. Directly below, a massive circular disk of fitted stone seals the floor of the chamber, its surface divided into rotating segments etched with star patterns.

**Based on:** Areas 5, 8 (lime mechanics), structural logic adapted
- The shaft descends roughly 40 feet into a circular chamber 30 feet across. The entire chamber is submerged. The stone disk in the floor is a sealed iris mechanism blocking access to Tier II.
- The walls and floor are coated in alkaline lime deposits. Direct skin contact with exposed stone for more than one round deals 1 acid damage per round. After 10 minutes of exposure, cloth and untreated leather begin degrading.
- The iris consists of six interlocking stone segments that can rotate. A DC 15 Investigation check reveals that three specific constellation symbols must be aligned to unlock the mechanism.
- If the mechanism is forced or misaligned, the iris opens partially and releases a powerful downward suction as drainage channels activate unpredictably. Creatures within 10 feet must succeed on a DC 14 Strength saving throw or be pulled downward 20 feet as the chamber begins to empty, taking 2d6 bludgeoning damage from tumbling debris before the iris reseals.
- If the correct alignment is completed, the iris opens fully and a concealed drainage system activates. Over the course of one minute, water is siphoned into hidden cisterns, emptying the shaft and chamber entirely.
- Once drained, the iris remains open and locked into place. The chamber below is revealed to be completely dry, with preserved stonework untouched by marine growth. A descending corridor leads deeper into Tier II. Once sealed, the pressure lock prevents seawater from re-entering unless the iris is deliberately sabotaged from below.

##### TIER II — THE CONSTELLATION LABYRINTH
_Completely dry. Architecturally preserved. Lower elevation but water-excluded._

###### C6. The Great Hall of Celestial Frescoes
>The drained shaft opens into a broad vaulted hall of clean, preserved stone. A massive mural dominates the eastern wall, depicting a calm ancient ocean beneath a radiant sun whose light pours into the depths. Two shallow alcoves flank the mural, each framed by carved tidal spirals and constellations. A wide stone passage continues onward through an arch to the south, while the sun in the mural seems carved slightly deeper than the surrounding stone.

**Based on:** TFtYP Area 15
- The hall is approximately 70 feet long and 30 feet wide with a 20-foot ceiling. The mural depicts the Couaxolotl presiding over a calm, stabilized sea; a DC 12 Religion or History check confirms it represents stewardship and protection.
- Each alcove contains a concealed floor plate. When a creature steps fully into an alcove, iron bars drop from ceiling slots and seal that alcove only, trapping anyone inside until released.
- The bars cannot be fully removed by force (DC 20 Athletics to lift enough to squeeze through). They retract only when the hidden mechanism in the mural is activated.
- A DC 15 Perception check reveals faint seams around the carved sun. Pressing the sun inward opens a concealed stone door within the mural and retracts any dropped bars.
- The secret door leads through a narrow side passage that reconnects beyond the primary hazard of the next chamber, allowing cautious explorers to bypass it. The main archway to the south leads directly into area C7.

###### C7. Hall of the Celestial Emblems
>The passage narrows into a long corridor where four massive axolotl-head reliefs jut from the walls like ceremonial masks. Their mouths hang open in rigid stone smirks, and something metallic glints in the throat of the far-right carving. The corridor continues onward beyond the reliefs.

**Based on:** TFtYP Area 17
- The corridor is straight and clear, with four large wall reliefs spaced along it. One relief has a visible bracelet lodged deep in its open mouth, positioned to tempt a hand or tool.
- A DC 15 Perception check spots fine scoring around the mouth edges and hairline seams in the jaw, suggesting it’s a moving mechanism rather than a static carving.
- Reaching into the mouth or attempting to extract the bracelet triggers the trap: the stone jaws snap shut on the intruding limb. The target must succeed on a DC 15 Dexterity saving throw or take the trap’s damage and become restrained by the jaws.
- While restrained, the creature continues taking damage at the start of each of its turns until freed. Forcing the jaws open requires a DC 20 Athletics check, and attacking the mechanism is possible but risks harming the trapped creature (run it like a crushing clamp).
- **Treasure**. The golden circlet is a bracelet of rock magic that was originally a ring, an earring, or some other piece of stone giant jewelry. 

###### C8. Star-Sand Gauntlet
>The corridor opens into a square chamber of smooth stone blocks, its ceiling pierced with hundreds of tiny star-shaped holes. The floor appears seamless, but faint drifts of pale, powder-fine sand gather in the corners. A stone doorway stands directly opposite the entrance, framed in carved tidal spirals. The air here feels unnaturally still.

**Based on:** TFtYP Area 24
- The chamber is 30 feet by 30 feet with a 20-foot ceiling. A concealed pressure plate spans the central 10-foot square of the floor.
- A DC 15 Perception check reveals hairline seams around the central stones and faint scrape marks near the ceiling vents, suggesting a mechanical function.
- When sufficient weight crosses the center, iron portcullises drop over both the entrance and the far exit, sealing the chamber completely. One round after the portcullises fall, fine pale “star-sand” begins pouring from the ceiling perforations, rising at a rate of 2 feet per round.
- At 6 feet deep, the sand becomes difficult terrain. At 10 feet, Medium creatures risk becoming restrained (DC 14 Strength save each round to move). When the chamber fills, creatures begin suffocating per normal rules.
- The portcullises can be lifted with a DC 20 Athletics check, and multiple creatures may cooperate. The sand stops pouring once one portcullis is raised and begins draining through hidden floor grates.
- The dust that fills the air as the sand falls causes choking. Unless it need not breathe, a creature in the dust must make a DC 13 Constitution saving throw at the start of its turn. On a failed save, the creature spends its turn coughing, able only to move at half speed or to make a check (with disadvantage) to free itself from the restrained condition. 
- If the secret passage from Room 6 is used, characters may enter from beyond the trap, avoiding activation entirely and potentially assisting trapped allies.

###### C9. The Court of the Tidal Game
>The corridor opens into a long stone court, its walls carved with graceful axolotls striking a heavy ball with sweeping tails. At both ends of the chamber, five feet above the floor, smooth hemispherical stone sockets are set into the walls like opposing goals. Resting in the exact center of the court is a dark stone sphere etched with tidal spirals and constellations.

**Based on:** TFtYP Area 29
- The chamber is a ritual ball court approximately 60 feet long and 30 feet wide. The sloped walls and paired stone sockets at each end function as opposing goals, preserving the two-sided structure of the original encounter. The carved reliefs depict axolotls playing the sacred game with their tails in fluid, circular motions.
- The stone ball (1-foot diameter, roughly 150 pounds) rests openly at the center of the court. When touched or struck, it springs upward, hovers, and animates to begin the ritual game. Ball's stats: fly 30 ft, hover; +5 melee; AC 13; 50 HP; limited damage immunities; can be grappled/restrained like an object; +5 to escape).
- Start of the game: roll initiative. The ball initially bounces/strikes at characters, trying to provoke hits back; on each hit it rebounds off the south wall and the southern goal briefly glows. After the second such hit, it stops attacking and a “trumpet” sound signals the match. Both goals (the southern socket above the pit and a second goal at the northern end of the hall, 140 feet away) glow orange until the game ends; when characters hit the ball it flies south, when it moves on its own it flies north.
- How the characters score: a successful hit sends the ball up to 15 feet south. To score in the southern goal, the ball must be within 15 feet of it and the player must declare the scoring attempt; if the attack roll exceeds the ball’s AC by 4+, it goes into the goal. 
- How the ball scores: if it gets within 5 feet of the northern wall, it can bounce itself into the northern goal by making a successful attack roll against AC 15. Once the ball enters either goal, it sticks there for 1 round and can’t be removed without destroying it.
- Stakes and win condition: if all characters fail to hit the ball for 1 round, a faint drum dirge is heard (pressure/taunt). If the ball scores in the northern goal, magic missiles erupt equal to the number of conscious characters; each missile hits a different character for 3 (1d4+1) force. Play continues until the characters die or they score enough to be 2 points ahead of the ball. 

###### C10. Foyer of Silver Reflection
>A narrow corridor ends at a tall hanging mirror framed in carved constellations, and a heavy glyph-covered stone door stands beside it. Beyond the door lies a circular chapel: a jade axolotl-shaped mask hangs on the south wall, a cross-shaped dais rises at the center, and low stone shelves sit in the inner corners of the cross. On the north landing of the dais stands a motionless armored warrior statue, its blade lowered toward the floor.

**Based on:** TFtYP Area 42
- **The Mirror**. The first creature to come within 10 feet of the mirror must make a DC 15 Wisdom saving throw. On a failure, it hallucinates a radiant winged axolotl-serpent emerging from the glass and attacking. In reality, the creature stands paralyzed and unresponsive. The effect lasts up to 1 minute; the creature may repeat the save if physically shaken or harmed.
- **The Glyph Door**. The heavy stone door opens into the chapel. The glyph carvings depict an ancient couatl protecting the seas and imprisoning those who sought to exploit divine power. This is purely narrative and has no mechanical trigger.
- **The Jade Mask**. The mask (worth 25 gp, weight 30 lb) hangs openly on a lever peg. Removing it causes the lever to pivot upward and three sets of iron bars to drop, caging the creature standing directly before it. The bars can be bent or lifted with a DC 20 Strength (Athletics) check.
- **The Offerings**. The shelves contain ceremonial jewelry and carved objects totaling approximately 450 gp in value. Removing offerings without caution triggers the guardian.
- **The Guardian**. The armored statue on the north landing is a Helmed Horror. It animates if the mask is removed, offerings are taken, or the chapel is otherwise desecrated. It fights until intruders withdraw or it is destroyed.
- A passage behind the dais leads deeper into the shrine.

`encounter: 1: Helmed Horror`

##### TIER III — INNER TEMPLE OF THE COUAXOLOTL
_Deepest level. Fully dry. Structurally perfect._

###### C11. Guardians Bar the Way
>The corridor narrows into a straight passage lined on both sides with life-sized stone warriors standing shoulder to shoulder, each gripping a long halberd. At the far end, a pair of bronze doors stands closed, their surface carved with spiraling tidal patterns. The floor stones here are smoother than those behind you.

**Based on:** Area 34
- The corridor is approximately 30 feet long and 10 feet wide. The stone warriors are carved in high relief along the walls, their halberds set into concealed pivoting mounts.
- A pressure plate occupies a 10-foot-square section of the floor roughly midway down the passage. A DC 15 Perception check reveals faint seams outlining the plate. When more than 30 pounds of weight rests on the plate, the halberds of the two nearest warriors swing inward and cross violently across the corridor. The pressure plate can be wedged or disabled with a DC 15 Dexterity (thieves’ tools) check.
- A creature touching or struck by a halberd takes lightning damage (2d4) and must succeed on a DC 15 Constitution saving throw or become paralyzed while in contact with the weapon. While paralyzed and touching the halberd, the creature takes the lightning damage again at the start of each of its turns. The halberds remain locked in a crossed position for 1 minute before resetting. While crossed, they block most of the passage; a Medium creature may attempt to crawl under them with a DC 10 Dexterity (Acrobatics) check to avoid contact.
- The bronze double doors at the end of the corridor are unlocked and lead to Room 12.

###### 12. The Miniature City of Khalesh
>The corridor opens into a square chamber centered on a waist-high stone platform. Upon it rests a miniature city carved from pale stone, its towers smooth and luminous, arranged in flowing, spiral forms. Thin channels of silvery liquid run between the buildings like canals. Against the far wall stands a sealed stone sarcophagus.

**Based on:** Area 33
- The miniature city represents an ancient couatl metropolis in Khalesh during the height of Irian’s influence. Its smooth, radiant architecture contrasts with the harsher stonework of the shrine.
- The silvery liquid flowing through the canals is molten metal. Touching it deals `dice:2d6` radiant damage. The metal remains fluid within the model but cools and crumbles into useless slag one minute after removal.
- Disturbing the model, removing pieces, or interfering with the molten channels triggers a glyph of warding centered on the platform. The glyph creates a circular wall of fire that can isolate creatures standing near the pedestal.
- The sarcophagus contains a concealed doppelganger. When the model is disturbed or the glyph activates, the doppelganger emerges and attempts to isolate a single target amid the confusion. The doppelganger fights intelligently and retreats if reduced below half hit points.
- A passage beyond the sarcophagus continues deeper into the shrine.

`encounter: 1: Doppelganger`

###### 13. The Vigil of the Last Titan
>The passage opens into a square chamber centered on a low marble slab. Upon it lies the preserved body of a massive giant clad in lacquered armor and copper-wire adornments, its hands wrapped around a long bronze-hafted spear shaped like a breaking wave. Simple jewelry and carved ornaments are scattered loosely around the slab. Two tall stone urns stand against the north wall, filled with smooth river stones.

**Based on:** Area 49
- The giant appears dead but perfectly preserved. Its armor is ceremonial rather than corroded, and faint sigils are etched into the spear shaft and the bier beneath it.
- The scattered jewelry on the floor consists of low-value offerings totaling approximately 80 gp if gathered. They are not trapped.
- The two urns are filled with river stones concealing more valuable treasure beneath them. Removing the stones reveals silver masks, bracelets, hairpins, and other valuables totaling several hundred gold pieces.
- The giant animates if any of the following occur: the spear is disturbed or removed; the slab is damaged; the urns are overturned; any of the visible offerings are taken; or any player attempts to leave the room back the way they came.
- When animated, the giant fights as a stone or hill giant equivalent (your choice based on party level), using the spear as its primary weapon. It does not leave the chamber.
- The giant ceases attacking if all removed items are returned to their original positions and the party withdraws 10 feet from the slab.
- A stone doorway beyond the bier leads onward to the final chamber of this tier.

###### 14. Chamber of the Radiant Current (Exit Mechanism)
>The corridor opens into a vast circular chamber beneath a high domed ceiling. At its center rises a carved stone pillar etched with spiraling constellations and tidal sigils. A deep circular trench surrounds the pillar, its walls worn smooth as if shaped by violent currents. Four narrow stone bridges span the trench and meet at the base of the pillar. Set into the pillar at chest height is a luminous prismatic pearl, glowing softly in radiant hues.

**Based on:** Area 53
- The chamber is approximately 60 feet in diameter. The trench is 15 feet deep with smooth vertical walls; climbing out requires a DC 15 Athletics check.
- The Pearl rests in a simple cradle. Removing it requires an action and immediately activates the ancient mechanism. The moment the Pearl is removed, a thunderous surge erupts from below. A 10-foot-wide vertical jet of seawater blasts upward from the trench through the pillar and into a vertical shaft in the ceiling.
- Creatures within 20 feet of the trench when the jet activates may attempt a DC 15 Dexterity saving throw to dive clear. On a failure, they are pulled into the trench and immediately caught in the jet.
- A creature inside the jet is violently propelled upward through a 200-foot vertical shaft. At the start of each of its turns while inside the jet, it must succeed on a DC 14 Strength saving throw or take `dice:3d6` bludgeoning damage from battering currents. A creature that willingly leaps into the jet makes this saving throw with advantage during the first round.
- The ascent lasts 3 rounds before depositing creatures into the flooded upper level of the shrine near the entrance.
- A creature that cannot breathe underwater and fails a Strength saving throw while inside the jet loses the ability to hold its breath due to the violent torrent and begins drowning.
	- **Drowning**. When a creature runs out of breath or is choking, it can survive for a number of rounds equal to its Constitution modifier (minimum of 1 round). At the start of its next turn, it drops to 0 hit points and is dying, and it can’t regain hit points or be stabilized until it can breathe again.
- After activation, the jet stabilizes into a steady upward current and remains active indefinitely, serving as a permanent return path to the shrine’s upper flooded level.
